Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_01.plot: On the day of governess Miss Taylor's wedding to Mr Weston, Emma and her father dine alone lamenting her absence until Mr Knightley arrives; Emma boasts of having engineered the match and declares she will next find a wife for Mr Elton, prompting Knightley to rebuke her interference.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_02.plot: Chapter 2 recounts Mr. Weston's backstory — his first marriage to Miss Churchill, their son Frank's adoption by the Churchill family, his rise to prosperity and second marriage to Miss Taylor — while Highbury eagerly anticipates Frank Churchill's long-promised visit, and Mrs. Weston settles happily into Randalls as Mr. Woodhouse continues to mourn her departure.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_03.plot: Emma meets Harriet Smith at a Hartfield evening party and, charmed by her beauty and deference, resolves to befriend, improve, and detach her from the socially inferior Martin family connections.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_04.plot: Emma cultivates her friendship with Harriet, dismisses Robert Martin as a socially unsuitable farmer after they briefly meet on the road, and schemes to redirect Harriet's affections toward Mr Elton as a far more appropriate match.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_05.plot: Mr. Knightley and Mrs. Weston debate the wisdom of Emma's friendship with Harriet Smith, with Knightley arguing it will harm both women while Mrs. Weston defends Emma's good character, ending with speculation about Emma's romantic future.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_06.plot: Emma orchestrates a portrait-sitting of Harriet while Mr Elton's obsequious admiration of the painting reveals his attachment — which Emma misreads as directed at Harriet rather than herself — and he volunteers to take the finished picture to London to be framed.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_07.plot: Robert Martin sends Harriet a marriage proposal by letter, but Emma steers Harriet into refusing it by appealing to social class distinctions and hinting at Mr Elton's attentions, then effectively writes the rejection letter herself.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_08.plot: Mr Knightley tells Emma that Robert Martin intends to propose to Harriet, only to learn Harriet has already refused him, triggering a heated argument in which Knightley accuses Emma of engineering the refusal and warns her that her scheme to match Harriet with Mr Elton will fail, while Emma dismisses his objections and is ultimately reassured when Harriet returns cheerfully with gossip hinting that Elton has gone to London on a mysterious errand involving a lady.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_09.plot: Mr Elton delivers a charade ("courtship") to Emma and Harriet; Emma misreads it as Elton's declaration of love for Harriet and enthusiastically transcribes it into Harriet's riddle book, convinced her matchmaking scheme is succeeding.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_10.plot: Emma and Harriet walk past Mr Elton's vicarage on a charitable visit, during which Emma declares her intention never to marry, dismisses Jane Fairfax as tiresome, and then deliberately engineers two opportunities — a pretended boot repair and a contrived visit to the vicarage — to leave Harriet and Mr Elton alone together, though no declaration results.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_11.plot: The John Knightley family arrives at Hartfield for a visit, and conversation turns to Mrs. Weston's new life and Frank Churchill, who is discussed but absent, known only through a congratulatory letter he sent from Weymouth.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_12.plot: Emma and Mr. Knightley reconcile after their quarrel over Harriet's rejection of Robert Martin, while a family evening at Hartfield dissolves into domestic squabbling over health advice and holiday choices, with Emma repeatedly steering conversation to prevent conflict.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_13.plot: Harriet falls ill and cannot attend the Westons' dinner at Randalls; Emma manipulates Mr. Elton to stay home (but fails), misinterprets his attentions toward herself as devotion to Harriet, and dismisses John Knightley's pointed warning that Elton is actually courting Emma.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_14.plot: At a dinner at the Westons', Emma endures Mr. Elton's unwanted attentions while learning from Mr. Weston that Frank Churchill plans to visit within a fortnight, a prospect that intrigues her greatly, though Mrs. Weston doubts the visit will happen given Mrs. Churchill's capricious temper.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_15.plot: Mr Elton, emboldened by wine, declares his love for Emma in the carriage home from Randalls, shocking her; she rejects him and realizes her matchmaking scheme for Harriet was wholly mistaken.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_16.plot: Emma reflects alone on Mr Elton's proposal, blaming herself for misleading Harriet, reassessing Elton's true mercenary character, and resolving to meddle no more—while winter weather conveniently keeps the parties apart.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_17.plot: Emma tells Harriet the truth about Mr Elton's departure and his lack of romantic interest in her, confesses her own matchmaking mistake, and resolves to comfort Harriet and suppress her own scheming imagination.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_18.plot: Frank Churchill fails to visit Randalls, and Emma and Mr Knightley argue sharply over whether Frank's absence reflects weakness of character or the genuine constraints of dependence on his aunt and uncle.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_19.plot: Emma and Harriet call on Miss Bates to escape talk of Mr Elton, and Emma learns through Miss Bates's voluble chatter that Jane Fairfax is coming to Highbury within the week, ill and unable to accompany the Campbells to Ireland, while Emma forms a suspicious theory about Jane's attachment to Mr Dixon.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_20.plot: Emma visits Miss Bates with Harriet to escape Harriet's obsessive talk of Mr Elton, only to be subjected to Miss Bates's lengthy chatter about a letter from Jane Fairfax announcing her imminent three-month visit to Highbury due to ill health, while Emma privately forms a suspicious theory about Jane and Mr Dixon.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_21.plot: Emma learns Jane Fairfax's history as an orphan raised by the Campbells, visits her after a two-year absence, briefly resolves to like her, but quickly relapses into irritation at Jane's cold reserve—especially regarding Frank Churchill and the Dixons.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_22.plot: Mr Knightley praises Emma's treatment of Jane Fairfax; Miss Bates arrives with news that Mr Elton is engaged to a Miss Hawkins of Bath; Harriet then arrives distressed after an accidental meeting with Robert Martin and his sister at Ford's shop, and Emma must comfort her while also breaking the Elton engagement news to distract her.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_23.plot: Mr Elton returns to Highbury triumphantly engaged to the wealthy Augusta Hawkins, while Emma reflects on her matchmaking blunder and manages Harriet's renewed heartbreak by arranging a brief, formal visit to the Martin family at Abbey Mill.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_24.plot: Frank Churchill arrives a day early at Highbury, meets Emma for the first time and makes a favorable impression, then departs to pay a visit to Jane Fairfax at Miss Bates's house; meanwhile Harriet endures a painful brief reunion with the Martin family.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_25.plot: Frank Churchill visits Highbury with Mrs. Weston, tours the village with Emma, discusses Jane Fairfax's reserve and her suspicious attachment to Mr. Dixon at Weymouth, enthuses about reviving balls at the Crown Inn, and inspects Mr. Elton's house with remarks suggesting his own desire for an early marriage.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_26.plot: Emma's opinion of Frank Churchill is shaken when he makes a frivolous trip to London for a haircut, while Mr. Knightley dismisses him as a trifling fellow; Emma then accepts an invitation to dine at the Coles' despite initial snobbish reluctance, learning that Harriet and Frank will attend, and persuading her anxious father to allow her to go.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_27.plot: At the Coles' dinner party, Emma and Frank Churchill gossip about the mysterious pianoforte gifted to Jane Fairfax, speculating it is from Mr. Dixon, while Mrs. Weston proposes that Mr. Knightley may be in love with Jane — a notion Emma vehemently rejects — before the evening ends with music, Frank singing alongside Emma, and an impromptu dance.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_28.plot: After reflecting on the Coles' dinner and her inferiority to Jane Fairfax at the pianoforte, Emma accompanies Harriet to Ford's shop, where she encounters Frank Churchill and Mrs. Weston, and is then invited by Miss Bates (who praises both Frank's helpfulness and Mr. Knightley's apple-giving generosity) to come hear the new instrument at the Bates's home.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_29.plot: Emma and Mrs. Weston visit Miss Bates's home where Frank Churchill repairs Mrs. Bates's spectacles and teasingly hints at Jane Fairfax's secret piano benefactor, while Mr. Knightley briefly stops outside on horseback, declines to come in, and the visit ends with Emma suspecting Jane harbors guilty feelings about the piano's mysterious donor.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_30.plot: Frank Churchill proposes moving the planned ball from Randalls to the Crown Inn, and he and Emma join the Westons to inspect the venue, debating room arrangements for supper and dancing, before Frank fetches Miss Bates and Jane Fairfax whose arrival resolves the indecision and secures Emma as Frank's partner for the first two dances.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_31.plot: Frank Churchill is abruptly recalled to Enscombe due to Mrs. Churchill's illness, cancelling the planned ball, and his emotional farewell leaves Emma half-convinced she is in love with him.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_32.plot: Emma coolly reassesses her feelings for Frank Churchill after reading his letter, schemes to redirect his affections toward Harriet, then must comfort the distressed Harriet over Mr. Elton's approaching wedding.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_33.plot: Emma and Harriet pay a wedding visit to Mrs Elton, whom Emma swiftly judges as vain, vulgar, and presumptuous; Mrs Elton's return visit to Hartfield confirms Emma's low opinion through insufferable comparisons to Maple Grove, unsolicited advice, and her familiar use of "Knightley," leaving Emma privately fuming and catching herself thinking of Frank Churchill.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_34.plot: Emma observes Mrs. Elton's overbearing patronage of Jane Fairfax, puzzles over Jane's mysterious refusal to leave Highbury, and during a conversation with Mr. Knightley and Mrs. Weston probes whether Knightley admires Jane romantically — he firmly denies any such intention while praising Jane's talents but noting her reserve.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_35.plot: Emma hosts a dinner party for the Eltons at Hartfield, where Jane Fairfax's insistence on fetching her own letters from the post-office (despite the rain and Mrs. Elton's overbearing offers to help) arouses Emma's suspicion that Jane is secretly corresponding with someone dear, and a debate over Frank Churchill's handwriting gives Emma a chance to test her own composure in speaking his name.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_36.plot: Mrs. Elton relentlessly pressures Jane Fairfax to seek a governess position, while Mr. Weston arrives with a letter announcing Frank Churchill's imminent return to the area, stirring agitation in Emma.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_37.plot: Mr. Weston announces Frank Churchill's imminent visit to London to Mrs. Elton, while Mr. John Knightley teases Emma about her increasingly busy social life and Mr. Knightley deflects Mrs. Elton's attempts at conversation.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_38.plot: Emma observes Frank Churchill's brief return visit, concludes his feelings for her have cooled, then learns the Churchills are moving to Richmond, enabling the long-planned Crown Inn ball to finally be arranged.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_39.plot: Emma observes that Frank Churchill's feelings for her have cooled during his brief visit, then learns Mrs. Churchill's move to Richmond brings Frank closer to Highbury, enabling the long-planned Crown Inn ball to finally be arranged.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_40.plot: At the Crown Inn ball, Mr Elton publicly snubs Harriet Smith by refusing to dance with her, but Mr Knightley rescues her by leading her to the set, and the chapter closes with Emma inviting Knightley to dance with her.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_41.plot: Frank Churchill rescues a terrified Harriet Smith from a gang of gypsies on the Richmond road and brings her to Hartfield, prompting Emma to fantasize that the incident will kindle a romance between them.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_42.plot: Harriet visits Emma to ceremonially burn her treasured relics of Mr. Elton (a scrap of court-plaister and a pencil stub), confessing she is over him, then reveals she has formed a new attachment to someone she considers far superior, whom Emma privately hopes is Frank Churchill but the text implies is Mr. Knightley.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_43.plot: Mr. Knightley grows suspicious of Frank Churchill's hidden connection with Jane Fairfax during an evening at Hartfield, where a word game with alphabet letters and a telling slip about Mr. Perry's carriage reveal covert signals between Frank and Jane, while Emma dismisses Knightley's warnings and insists there is no attachment between them.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_44.plot: The Donwell Abbey strawberry party takes place: Emma observes Knightley with Harriet near Abbey Mill Farm, Jane Fairfax slips away home in exhausted distress, and a hot, irritable Frank Churchill arrives late — prompting Emma to reflect she is glad she no longer loves him.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_45.plot: At the Box Hill picnic Emma flirts openly with Frank Churchill, cruelly mocks Miss Bates in public, and is afterwards rebuked by Mr Knightley, leaving her overwhelmed with shame and remorse on the drive home.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_46.plot: Emma visits Miss Bates to atone for her Box Hill rudeness, learns Jane Fairfax has accepted a governess post arranged by Mrs Elton, and hears that Frank Churchill has abruptly departed for Richmond.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_47.plot: Mr. Knightley departs for London after a warm but abrupt farewell with Emma; news arrives of Mrs. Churchill's sudden death, raising hopes for Frank and Harriet's attachment; Emma repeatedly attempts to offer kindness to the ailing Jane Fairfax, who refuses all assistance and pointedly excludes Emma while accepting others.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_48.plot: Mrs. Weston reveals to Emma that Frank Churchill has been secretly engaged to Jane Fairfax since October, and Emma — though initially horrified and morally indignant at Frank's duplicity — reassures Mrs. Weston she herself was never seriously attached to him, while privately pitying Harriet.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_49.plot: Emma learns that Harriet's secret admiration is for Mr Knightley, not Frank Churchill, forcing Emma to confront her own self-deception and realize she herself loves Mr Knightley.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_50.plot: Emma, tormented by the revelation that Harriet loves Mr Knightley, reflects on her own long-unacknowledged feelings for him, writes to keep Harriet away from Hartfield, then hears Mrs Weston's account of Jane Fairfax's painful confession about the secret engagement, and spends a miserable evening contemplating a future in which all her friends will be lost to her.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_51.plot: Mr. Knightley returns from London, walks with Emma in the garden, and after learning she never loved Frank Churchill, declares his own love for her — Emma accepts, and both realize they have been mutually in love all along.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_52.plot: Emma, elated after Mr. Knightley's proposal, reads Frank Churchill's long confessional letter to Mrs. Weston explaining his secret engagement to Jane Fairfax, his deceptive conduct, their quarrel, and their reconciliation, while Emma herself resolves to protect her father and handle Harriet by letter and removal to London.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_53.plot: Mr. Knightley reads Frank Churchill's explanatory letter aloud with Emma, offering sharp moral commentary, then proposes to Emma with a plan to move into Hartfield to spare Mr. Woodhouse, while Emma worries about the effect on Harriet.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_54.plot: Emma arranges for Harriet to go to London to ease her own guilt, then visits Jane Fairfax, where they exchange a private moment of mutual forgiveness and Jane confirms that her future with Frank Churchill at Enscombe is settled once mourning ends.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_55.plot: Emma and Mr. Knightley share tender reflections on their relationship, then Emma breaks news of their engagement to Mr. Woodhouse and later to Mrs. Weston, whose endorsement helps reconcile Mr. Woodhouse; the news spreads through Highbury via Miss Bates to mixed reactions, including Mr. Elton's indifference and Mrs. Elton's pronounced displeasure.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_56.plot: Mr. Knightley tells Emma that Harriet Smith has accepted Robert Martin's proposal, and Emma—secretly relieved—warmly approves; later at Randalls, Emma and Frank Churchill meet with Jane Fairfax, exchange forgiveness and playful banter, and Emma privately concludes that Mr. Knightley is far superior to Frank in character.

Testi/Austen/Atomized/Emma/Chapter_57.plot: Harriet's engagement to Robert Martin is confirmed and they marry; Harriet's illegitimate tradesman parentage is revealed; Emma and Mr Knightley finally fix their wedding date after Mr Woodhouse's anxiety is overcome by a poultry robbery, and they wed before the chapter closes with the novel's end.
